title: Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:1–11)
hookLine: a hard story about lying to the community
carry: the bible keeps the hard stories

cards: Founding stories tend to get polished. The brochure keeps the triumphs and quietly drops the rest. So this part of Acts surprises.

Luke has just described the first Christians in Jerusalem as one heart and one soul, sharing everything, so that no one among them was in need. A man named Barnabas sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet.
And right after that glowing picture, Luke tells a story that is very hard to read.

teach.b: A married couple, Ananias and Sapphira, sell a piece of land too. They keep back part of the money and bring the rest, presenting it as the whole. Nobody required them to sell, or to give it all.
Peter says so: while it remained, was it not yours? And after it was sold, wasn't the money in your power?
The problem isn't the amount. It's the pretending. Peter tells Ananias: "Thou hast not lied to men, but to God."
And Ananias falls down and dies. About three hours later Sapphira comes in, not knowing what has happened. Peter asks her straight: did you sell the land for so much?
She says yes, for so much. And she falls down and dies too.

Great fear came upon the whole church, Luke says: in Greek, the ekklēsia, the assembly. What do we do with a story like this? The text doesn't explain how they died, or say anything about their eternal fate.
Some readers see God's judgment; others see a shock so great it killed them. The passage itself doesn't settle it.
What it does show is that a community built on sharing can be poisoned by pretending, by people performing a generosity they don't have.
And Luke didn't leave it out.
The Church's founding story includes this, and Peter's denial, and the disciples' squabbles.
So ends week seventy-seven: feed my sheep, witness, Matthias, Peter's first sermon, silver and gold, we cannot but speak, and a hard story.

how: Catholics examine their conscience, often at night, and confess serious sins in the sacrament of penance; the early community's sharing in Acts 4 and 5 is read at Mass in the Easter season.

o: a Greek word for sudden fear or dread
the field Barnabas sold for the apostles
the assembly, Luke's word for the church

games.q: the hard story — tap the pairs.
p: sells a field and gives it all
thou hast not lied to men, but to God

s: the believers in Acts were required to give all their money
Peter says the land and the money were theirs to keep.
Ananias and Sapphira's wrong was the pretending, not the amount
they kept part back while presenting it as the whole.
the text explains exactly how they died
it says they fell down and died, and doesn't explain how.

games.q: you're Sapphira. three hours after your husband, you walk in. Peter asks, did you sell the land for so much? what do you say?
o: tell the truth: we kept part back.
games.why: she repeats the lie: yea, for so much. and she falls down too. Peter gave her the chance to tell the truth.

practice: Let one small pretense come to mind: saying fine when it isn't, a number rounded up, a story improved. No punishment, just honesty; picture setting the record straight, or simply not adding to it.
If you pray, bring it to God as it is, or think of it in light of the sacrament of confession; if you don't, just see it clearly.

wordCard.voice: Ekklēsia. Luke's word for the assembly of believers, seized by fear after Ananias and Sapphira's pretense was exposed. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: church, assembly. Luke's word at 5:11 for the believers seized by fear.
